recentItems.title: What's the Deal with Prior Authorizations?
recentItems.description:
Have you ever left a doctor’s appointment with a whole plan to tackle some health issue you’re facing, only to get a call later saying someone at your insurance company, who may or may not be a doctor, needs more information before they’ll approve coverage for this thing your doctor is certain you need?

That is the dreaded prior authorization, and it’s the topic of this week’s Healthcare Triage.

Learn more about prior authorizations with this AcademyHealth article: https://academyhealth.org/publications/2026-08/prior-authorization-reform-evidence-behind-debate-reforms-now-moving-and-what-no-one-measuring

recentItems.title: What's the Deal with Screen Time?
recentItems.description:

But is that the full story? We’re about to find out.

recentItems.title: Why Do Patients Have to Do So Much Admin Work?
recentItems.description:
Health care in the United States is expensive, and paying for it can get complicated. If you have insurance coverage, a lot of routine medical care is directly covered by that insurance, meaning all the payments take place between the provider and the insurance company. But sometimes patients have to pay out of pocket and get reimbursed by their insurance later. Maybe this has happened to you. If it has, you know it can be...painful.

recentItems.description:
The U.S. spends about 18% of its GDP on health care. That's nearly double what many other high-income countries spend, even though our health outcomes aren't better.
Meanwhile, public frustration is real. Surveys show many Americans feel the system isn't meeting their needs.

recentItems.description:

But when I watch the news, all I can think is that the pressure points aren't always where people think they are.

recentItems.title: How Does the US Spend So Much on Healthcare?
recentItems.description:
So here's the situation: the United States spends more on health care than basically anyone else on Earth, and somehow we're not healthier for it.

Like, not even a little bit more. In fact, compared to other high-income countries, we tend to have worse outcomes. I'm talking lower life expectancy, higher rates of avoidable death, more chronic disease.

Why is this happening, and what can we do about it?

recentItems.title: How Prior Authorizations Slow Down Treatments
recentItems.description:
Prior authorization is a process where your doctor has to get approval from your insurance company before you can receive certain treatments, tests, or medications, if you want them covered. If that approval doesn't happen, your insurer may not pay.

On paper, the idea is pretty straightforward. Insurers use prior authorization as a way to manage costs and make sure care is medically necessary, safe, and cost-effective. It's one of the most common tools used in U.S. healthcare to control the use of expensive or potentially avoidable services. So why do doctors and patients hate them so much?
